cubic.name: One cubic with its gradient, tangents and turning points
cubic.summary: Pick a and the stationary x-values p and q, build f′(x) = 3a(x − p)(x − q), add a constant d, then derive every linked quantity, at the turning points and at a chosen point x₀.

quantities.name: a
quantities.is: leading coefficient of f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d

quantities.name: p, q
quantities.is: the x-coordinates of the stationary points
quantities.pick: integers with p < q and |p|, |q| ≤ 4; a(p + q) even so b is a whole number; p + q even when the point of inflexion is asked

quantities.name: b, c, d
quantities.is: the other coefficients
quantities.pick: b = −3a(p + q)/2, c = 3apq, d a small integer

quantities.name: f′(x)
quantities.is: the gradient function 3ax² + 2bx + c
quantities.pick: 3a(x − p)(x − q)

quantities.name: f″(x)
quantities.is: the second derivative 6ax + 2b
quantities.pick: f″(p) = −3a(q − p) and f″(q) = 3a(q − p), so the signs are opposite

quantities.name: stationary points
quantities.is: (p, f(p)) and (q, f(q)): a local maximum and a local minimum
quantities.pick: from p and q; for a > 0 the left one is the maximum

quantities.name: point of inflexion
quantities.pick: midway between the stationary points

quantities.name: x₀
quantities.is: the point where the gradient, the tangent and the normal are asked
quantities.pick: small integer, not p or q, so f′(x₀) ≠ 0

quantities.name: tangent and normal at x₀
quantities.is: y = mx + c with m = f′(x₀) through (x₀, f(x₀)); the normal has gradient −1/m
quantities.pick: from f(x₀) and f′(x₀)

quantities.name: given gradient
quantities.is: a gradient g reached at two whole-number x-values r and s
quantities.pick: r + s = p + q and g = f′(r), with g ≠ 0

quantities.name: hidden coefficient
quantities.is: b or c written as k, found from the tangent's gradient at x₀
quantities.pick: b only when x₀ ≠ 0

concepts.prompt: The lines 2x + 3y = 6 and 3x − 2y = 1 are perpendicular.
concepts.answer: True. The gradients are −2/3 and 3/2, and (−2/3) × (3/2) = −1.

concepts.prompt: A straight line meets both axes.
concepts.answer: Sometimes. A horizontal line such as y = 3 never meets the x-axis, and a vertical line such as x = 2 never meets the y-axis. Every other line meets both (at the same point if it passes through the origin).

concepts.prompt: In ax + by + d = 0, d changes while a and b stay the same. What happens to the line?
concepts.answer: It slides without turning: the gradient −a/b does not change, so the new line is parallel to the old one. The intercepts −d/a and −d/b grow or shrink in step with d.

concepts.prompt: If f(2) = 5 and f has an inverse, then f⁻¹(5) = 2.
concepts.answer: True. The point (2, 5) is on f, so (5, 2) is on f⁻¹: the inverse sends each output back to the input that made it.

concepts.prompt: A table shows f(1) = 4, f(4) = 2 and f(2) = 7. Predict whether (f∘f)(1) equals f(1) × f(1). Then work it out.
concepts.answer: No. (f∘f)(1) = f(f(1)) = f(4) = 2, while f(1) × f(1) = 16. Composing feeds one output in as the next input; it does not multiply.

concepts.prompt: The graph of f rises steadily from (−2, 1) to (4, 7). State the domain and range of f⁻¹ and say why.
concepts.answer: Domain 1 ≤ x ≤ 7 and range −2 ≤ y ≤ 4. Every point (p, q) on f becomes (q, p) on f⁻¹, so the x-values and y-values swap roles.

concepts.prompt: A function and its inverse can only meet on the line y = x.
concepts.answer: False. f(x) = 2 − x is its own inverse, so its graph meets f⁻¹ at every point, and only (1, 1) is on y = x. For an increasing f, though, every meeting point is on y = x.

concepts.prompt: The inverse of an increasing function is increasing.
concepts.answer: Always. If a < b then f(a) < f(b). f⁻¹ sends f(a) back to a and f(b) back to b, so a bigger input to f⁻¹ still gives a bigger output.

concepts.prompt: f(x) = 2x − 3. Predict where the graphs of f and f⁻¹ meet. Then check.
concepts.answer: f is increasing, so they meet on y = x: 2x − 3 = x gives (3, 3). Check: f⁻¹(x) = (x + 3)/2 and f⁻¹(3) = 3.

concepts.answer: False. Those are only the end values. The vertex at x = 0 is inside the domain, so the smallest value is 0 and the range is 0 ≤ y ≤ 9.

concepts.prompt: Reflecting a graph in the x-axis leaves its range unchanged.
concepts.answer: Sometimes. Every output changes sign, so y ≥ 1 becomes y ≤ −1. The range stays the same only when it is balanced about 0, such as −2 ≤ y ≤ 2.

concepts.prompt: On −2 ≤ x ≤ 3, the greatest value of f(x) = x³ − 3x is at its local maximum.
concepts.answer: False. The local maximum is (−1, 2), but the endpoint gives f(3) = 27 − 9 = 18. On a closed domain, check the endpoints as well as the turning points.

concepts.prompt: Before graphing f(x) = ln(x + 1) − x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 6, predict how many zeros it has. Then check with the GDC.
concepts.answer: Two. f(0) = 0. Near 0 the log climbs faster than x/2 (slope 1 against 1/2), but in the end x/2 wins: f(6) = ln 7 − 3 ≈ −1.05. So the curve rises, turns at (1, 0.193) and comes back down through a second zero at x ≈ 2.51.

concepts.prompt: If a graph crosses the x-axis twice, it has a turning point between the two zeros.
concepts.answer: Sometimes. If the curve is unbroken between the zeros, it must turn to come back to the axis. Across a vertical asymptote it need not: y = x − 1/x has zeros −1 and 1, a break at x = 0, and no turning point at all.

concepts.prompt: v(t) = (t − 1)(t − 5) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Predict the values at both ends and the lowest point before sketching.
concepts.answer: Both ends give 5: v(0) = (−1)(−5) = 5 and v(6) = (5)(1) = 5. They match because 0 and 6 are the same distance from the axis t = 3. The lowest point is the vertex (3, −4).

concepts.prompt: y = 2 + 3e^(−x) for x ≥ 0 has a minimum value of 2.
concepts.answer: False. The curve falls towards y = 2 for ever but never reaches it, so there is no minimum value; the range is 2 < y ≤ 5. The level 2 is an asymptote, not a turning point.

concepts.prompt: A parabola's vertex is the same point as its y-intercept.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: only when the axis of symmetry is x = 0, as for y = x² − 4. For y = (x − 1)(x − 5) the vertex is (3, −4) but the y-intercept is (0, 5).

concepts.answer: False. Each year multiplies by 1.1, so two years multiply by 1.1² = 1.21: a 21% rise. The second 10% is taken of a bigger amount.

concepts.prompt: If the common difference d is negative, the sum Sₙ is negative for every large enough n.
concepts.answer: True. Sₙ = n/2 (2u₁ + (n − 1)d), and the bracket keeps falling by d for each extra term, so it becomes negative and stays negative.

concepts.prompt: For an arithmetic sequence of whole numbers, Sₙ is a multiple of n.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: Sₙ = n × (u₁ + uₙ)/2, so it is a multiple of n exactly when u₁ + uₙ is even.

concepts.prompt: A thing that loses 10% of its value each year has lost 30% of its value after 3 years.
concepts.answer: False: each 10% is of the value at the start of that year, which keeps falling. It keeps 0.9^3 = 0.729 of its value, so it has lost 27.1%.

concepts.prompt: Under a fixed percentage depreciation, the loss in each year is smaller than the loss in the year before.

concepts.answer: 8000 is the value when t = 0, the price paid. 0.92 is the fraction kept each year, so the value falls by 8% a year.

concepts.prompt: Compounding more often a year always gives a larger value than compounding annually, at the same annual rate.
concepts.answer: Always: at the same nominal rate each period's interest starts earning interest sooner, so the yearly growth factor (1 + r/100k)^k rises with k. At 5% it is 1.0500 annually, 1.0509 quarterly and 1.0512 monthly.

concepts.prompt: $1000 invested at 5% compounded annually for 10 years earns twice as much interest as $1000 invested at 5% for 5 years.
concepts.answer: False: interest is earned on interest, so the second five years earn more than the first. The 10-year interest is $628.89 and the 5-year interest is $276.28, more than double.

concepts.prompt: An investment that is worth $5000 after 3 years at 4% compounded annually is worth $5000 ÷ 1.04^3 now.
concepts.answer: True: the value after 3 years is PV × 1.04^3, so the amount invested now is the future value divided by 1.04^3.

concepts.prompt: The sum of three consecutive integers is divisible by 6.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: the sum is 3(n + 1), a multiple of 3 every time, but it needs n + 1 even to be a multiple of 6. 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 works and 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 does not.

concepts.answer: False: n + 3/2 is not an integer, so the 6 outside proves nothing. At n = 1, 6n + 9 = 15, which is not a multiple of 6.

concepts.prompt: A quota sample and a stratified sample of the same size contain the same numbers from each group, so they are the same method.
concepts.answer: False: the numbers match, but a stratified sample draws at random inside each group, and a quota sample takes whoever comes by until each group is full.

concepts.prompt: A larger sample gets rid of bias.
concepts.answer: Never by itself: more people from the same biased method makes the result steadier, not fairer. Only changing who can be chosen removes the bias.

concepts.prompt: If a sample is random, its mix of groups matches the population.
concepts.answer: False: a random method gives everyone a fair chance, but chance can still move any one sample away from the true mix.

concepts.prompt: A cumulative frequency of 30 at x = 20 means that 30 values are equal to 20.
concepts.answer: False: it is a running total, so 30 values are at or below 20.

concepts.prompt: The 90th percentile is read across from 90 on the vertical axis.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: only when n is 100. Otherwise it is across from 90% of n.

concepts.prompt: The curve is steepest between 20 and 30. What does that say about the data?
concepts.answer: More values lie in that stretch than in any other of the same width: steep means many, flat means few.

concepts.prompt: In a box plot, the longest whisker holds the most data.
concepts.answer: False: each whisker and each half of the box holds about a quarter of the data. A long section means those values are spread out, not that there are more of them.

concepts.prompt: The median is in the middle of the box.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: it is only when the data between the quartiles are symmetric. The median splits the data in two by count, not the box by length.

concepts.prompt: A box plot has a long upper whisker. Predict whether the mean is above or below the median, then say why.
concepts.answer: Above: the median depends only on the middle of the data, but the mean uses every value, so the few high values pull it up.

concepts.prompt: The mean found from a grouped table is the exact mean of the data.
concepts.answer: False: the table hides where in each class the values lie, so every value is replaced by its mid-interval value. The result is an estimate.

concepts.prompt: A standard deviation can be negative when most of the values are below the mean.
concepts.answer: False: the deviations are squared before they are added, and the standard deviation is the positive root of the result.

concepts.prompt: The mean of two groups together is the average of their two means.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: only when the groups are the same size, or have the same mean. Otherwise the larger group pulls the mean its way.

concepts.prompt: The mean of a data set is one of the values in the data set.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: for 2, 4, 6 the mean is 4, which is in the set, but for 1, 2, 6 the mean is 3, which is not.

concepts.prompt: The median of an ordered data set with 12 values is the 6th value.
concepts.answer: False: with an even number of values the median is halfway between the 6th and 7th values, so it need not be a value in the set.

concepts.prompt: One class of 10 students has a mean mark of 60 and another of 30 students has a mean mark of 80. The mean mark of all 40 students is 70.
concepts.answer: False: the mean of the two means ignores the group sizes. The totals are 600 and 2400, so the mean is 3000 ÷ 40 = 75, nearer the bigger group's mean.

concepts.prompt: If y = 3x + 40 is a regression line, then every extra unit of x adds exactly 3 to y for each individual.
concepts.answer: False: 3 is an average rate for the data. Real points sit above and below the line, so one individual may change by more or by less.

concepts.prompt: The value of b in y = ax + b is a sensible estimate of y at x = 0.
concepts.answer: Sometimes: it is when x = 0 is in the data and the value is possible. If x = 0 is far outside the data, b is an extrapolation and may mean nothing.

concepts.prompt: Predict y at x = 10 and at x = 11 on a line y = ax + b. What is the difference?
concepts.answer: It is exactly a, whatever x you start from: this is what the gradient means.

concepts.prompt: If A and B are mutually exclusive and neither has probability 0, then they are independent.
concepts.answer: False: if A happens then B can't, so knowing A changes the probability of B completely. P(A ∩ B) = 0, but P(A) × P(B) is not 0.

concepts.prompt: Two independent events can't happen together.
concepts.answer: False: that describes mutually exclusive events. Independent events with non-zero probabilities always overlap, because P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) is not 0.

concepts.prompt: If A and B are independent, then A′ and B′ are independent.

concepts.prompt: √(x²) = x for every real x.
concepts.answer: False. √((−3)²) = √9 = 3, not −3; in fact √(x²) = |x|. Squaring sends 3 and −3 to the same output, so √ can only undo it on x ≥ 0. That is why x² must be cut to x ≥ 0 before √x is its inverse.

concepts.prompt: (f∘g)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.
concepts.answer: Sometimes, but not in general. To undo "g then f" you undo f first, so (f∘g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹∘f⁻¹. With f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, (f∘g)⁻¹(x) = (x − 1)/2, but f⁻¹(g⁻¹(x)) = x/2 − 1.

concepts.prompt: The average cost of making n items is A(n) = 4 + 500/n dollars. What do 4 and 500 mean?
concepts.answer: 500 is the fixed cost in dollars, shared over n items, and 4 is the cost of each extra item. As n grows the fixed cost is spread thinner, so A(n) falls towards 4.

concepts.prompt: If A(n) = 4 + 500/n, enough items will bring the average cost down to exactly $4.
concepts.answer: False. 500/n is positive for every n, so A(n) > 4 always. It gets as close as you like to 4 but never reaches it.

concepts.prompt: For A(n) = 4 + 500/n, predict whether 166 items are enough to bring the average cost below $7. Then check.
concepts.answer: No. 500/n < 3 needs n > 166.7, so the least number is 167. Check: A(166) ≈ 7.01 and A(167) ≈ 6.99.

concepts.prompt: An equation that is true for x = 1 and for x = 2 is an identity.
concepts.answer: Sometimes. x² = 3x − 2 is true at x = 1 and x = 2 but not at x = 0 (0 ≠ −2), so it is only an equation. An identity must hold for every x.

concepts.prompt: Predict which form of cos 2x turns cos 2x + 3 sin x − 2 = 0 into a quadratic in one function, then solve for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
concepts.answer: 1 − 2sin²x, because the rest of the equation is in sin x. Then 2sin²x − 3 sin x + 1 = 0, so (2 sin x − 1)(sin x − 1) = 0 and x = π/6, π/2 or 5π/6.

concepts.prompt: The greatest value of a function on a closed interval is always at a stationary point.
concepts.answer: False. It can be at an endpoint. On 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, f(x) = x² − 4x + 1 has its only stationary point at (2, −3), a minimum; the greatest value is f(5) = 6.

concepts.prompt: Why does "the line is a tangent to the parabola" mean the discriminant is zero?
concepts.answer: Equating the line and the curve gives a quadratic whose roots are the x-values where they meet. A tangent meets the curve at exactly one point, so there is one repeated root, and that happens when Δ = 0. Δ > 0 means two meeting points; Δ < 0 means none.

concepts.prompt: Predict the greatest and least values of y = 4 sin(3x) − 1 without calculus. Then check with dy/dx = 0.
concepts.answer: 3 and −5: sin is between −1 and 1, so 4 sin(3x) is between −4 and 4, then subtract 1. dy/dx = 12 cos(3x) = 0 where sin(3x) = ±1, giving the same values.

types.name: Area under a curve above the x-axis
types.summary: Write the integral for a shaded area above the x-axis (its limits and integrand), then evaluate it.
types.gap: Bank area parts (t5-definite-integral-area, t5-area-between-curves) involve regions below the axis or between two curves; the basic area above the axis is not a type of its own.

types.name: The second derivative in context
types.summary: Say what the sign of the second derivative means in context, such as "the temperature is rising, but more and more slowly".
types.gap: Bank concavity parts (t5-concavity) compute f″ or match graphs; none interprets it in context.

types.name: Greatest and least values on an interval
types.summary: Find the greatest and least values of f on a closed interval by comparing the stationary values with the values at the endpoints, and state the range.
types.gap: Endpoints appear in GDC sketches and once inside a kinematics chain (comparing an endpoint with a local maximum), but no exam type is built on finding the greatest and least values of f on an interval.

types.name: Constants from a stationary point
types.summary: Find unknown constants in f given a stationary point or a point of inflexion, using f′ = 0 (or f″ = 0) together with the point itself.
types.gap: Bank stationary-point parts start from a known function; none works backwards to its constants.

types.name: Integrate using a derivative ("hence")
types.summary: Differentiate a given expression, then use the result to integrate a related function, adjusting the constant factor.
types.gap: Bank integration parts (t5-indefinite-integral) use standard results or inspection; none links back to a derivative found just before.

types.name: Properties of definite integrals
types.summary: Use the rules for definite integrals of an unknown f: reverse the limits, split the interval, take out a constant factor, and add a constant to the integrand.
types.gap: Bank definite-integral parts (t5-definite-integral-area) evaluate integrals of known functions; none uses the properties on an unknown f.
